sentence: The man ___ lives next door is a doctor.
explanation: 'Who' refers to people as the subject of the clause; 'which' is for things and 'whose' shows possession.

sentence: A nurse is a person ___ looks after patients.
explanation: 'Who' introduces a defining clause about a person performing the action.

sentence: The woman ___ won the prize gave a short speech.
explanation: The gap is the subject pronoun for a person, so 'who' is needed; 'whose' would show possession.

sentence: Students ___ hand in their essays late will lose marks.
explanation: 'Who' refers to the students performing the action; the verb 'will lose' follows later in the sentence.

sentence: The police have arrested the man ___ stole the painting.
explanation: 'Who' is the subject relative pronoun for people in defining clauses.

sentence: The girl ___ sits behind me in class is from Peru.
explanation: 'Who' refers to a person who is the subject; 'which' refers only to things.

sentence: Anyone ___ wants to join the trip should sign up today.
explanation: 'Anyone who' is the standard pattern; 'who' is the subject pronoun for people.

sentence: The people ___ moved in upstairs are very quiet.
explanation: 'Who' is the subject relative pronoun for people; 'whose' would need a noun after it.

sentence: The book ___ I borrowed from the library is two weeks overdue.
explanation: 'Which' refers to things; 'who' refers only to people and 'where' to places.

sentence: The river ___ runs through the town often floods in spring.
explanation: 'Which' is the subject relative pronoun for things and animals.

sentence: The programme ___ I watched last night was about volcanoes.
explanation: 'Which' refers to things, even when it is the object of the clause.

sentence: The house ___ stands on the corner dates from 1870.
explanation: 'Which' is needed because a house is a thing; 'where' would introduce information about location, not a subject.

sentence: The company ___ produces these parts has factories in three countries.
explanation: A company takes 'which' as subject; 'who' is normally reserved for individual people.

sentence: The train ___ leaves at six is usually very crowded.
explanation: 'Which' is the subject pronoun for things; the clause sits between the subject 'train' and its verb 'is'.

sentence: The letter ___ arrived this morning is from my aunt.
explanation: 'Which' refers to the letter, a thing, as the subject of 'arrived'.

sentence: We stayed in a hotel ___ overlooked the harbour.
explanation: Here the hotel does the action ('overlooked'), so 'which' is needed, not 'where'.

sentence: My uncle, ___ lives in Canada, is coming to stay next week.
hint: non-defining clause after a comma about a person
explanation: In non-defining clauses (between commas) 'that' is not allowed; 'who' refers to people.

sentence: Mrs Patterson, ___ taught me maths, has just retired.
hint: extra information after a comma about a person
explanation: After a comma the relative clause is non-defining, so 'that' is impossible and 'who' refers to the person.

sentence: Pablo, ___ speaks five languages, works as an interpreter.
explanation: Non-defining clauses about people take 'who'; 'that' never follows a comma in standard English.

sentence: The director, ___ we met at the conference, has written to us.
hint: person as object, but the clause is non-defining
explanation: In non-defining clauses 'that' cannot replace 'who', even when the person is the object.

sentence: Anna's father, ___ is a dentist, has offered to check my teeth.
hint: extra information about a person between commas
explanation: Non-defining relative clauses about people use 'who' as subject; 'that' is wrong after a comma.

sentence: Our new neighbours, ___ have three children, moved in last week.
hint: people as subject; clause between commas
explanation: 'Who' is used for people in non-defining clauses; 'which' is for things.

sentence: The winner, ___ was only seventeen, broke the championship record.
hint: person as subject after a comma
explanation: The clause adds extra information about a person, so 'who' is required and 'that' is impossible.

sentence: My colleague Anna, ___ joined us in May, has already been promoted.
explanation: 'Who' refers to Anna; non-defining clauses never use 'that'.

sentence: The Eiffel Tower, ___ attracts millions of visitors, was completed in 1889.
explanation: For things in non-defining clauses use 'which'; 'that' is not allowed after a comma.

sentence: The new bridge, ___ cost two billion euros, opened last month.
hint: thing + extra information after a comma
explanation: 'Which' introduces non-defining clauses about things; 'that' is forbidden there.

sentence: This clock, ___ belonged to my grandmother, is still working perfectly.
hint: thing as subject; clause between commas
explanation: The clock is a thing, so 'which' is correct; 'that' cannot be used in a non-defining clause.

sentence: The company's shares, ___ rose sharply yesterday, are still undervalued.
explanation: 'Which' refers to the shares; 'that' is impossible in a clause set off by commas.

sentence: The house at the end of the street, ___ has been empty for years, is for sale.
explanation: Non-defining clauses about things take 'which'; 'who' is for people and 'that' is not allowed here.

sentence: His latest film, ___ was shot entirely in Iceland, won three awards.
explanation: 'Which' is the subject pronoun for the film; 'that' never appears in non-defining clauses.

sentence: The Blue Train, ___ runs between Pretoria and Cape Town, is famous for its luxury.
explanation: For a thing in a non-defining clause use 'which'; 'that' cannot follow the comma.

sentence: Mount Everest, ___ was first climbed in 1953, attracts hundreds of climbers every year.
explanation: 'Which' introduces extra information about the mountain; 'that' is wrong after a comma.

sentence: He passed all his exams first time, ___ surprised everyone.
hint: refers to the whole previous clause
explanation: 'Which' can refer to a whole idea ('he passed first time'); this non-defining use never takes 'that'.

sentence: She was two hours late, ___ annoyed the interviewer.
hint: comment on the whole situation before the comma
explanation: When a clause comments on the whole previous statement, use 'which' after the comma.

sentence: The shower suddenly stopped working, ___ meant we had to call a plumber.
hint: refers back to the whole event
explanation: 'Which' refers to the whole preceding clause; 'what' cannot introduce this kind of clause after a comma.

sentence: They said nothing at all, ___ I found rather strange.
explanation: 'Which' here means 'and this'; it refers to the whole situation and follows a comma.

sentence: The woman ___ car was stolen reported it immediately.
explanation: 'Whose' shows possession (her car); 'who's' means 'who is' and would be ungrammatical here.

sentence: That's the boy ___ dog won first prize at the show.
hint: the dog belongs to the boy
explanation: 'Whose dog' means 'his dog'; 'who's' would mean 'who is', which makes no sense here.

sentence: The author ___ books sell millions worldwide lives in Iceland.
explanation: 'Whose' links the author to her books; 'who' could not be followed directly by 'books'.

sentence: We interviewed a candidate ___ references were excellent.
hint: the references belong to the candidate
explanation: 'Whose references' means 'the candidate's references', so the possessive relative 'whose' is needed.

sentence: The man ___ wallet I found works at the post office.
explanation: 'Whose wallet' means 'the man's wallet'; 'who's' means 'who is' and cannot precede a noun.

sentence: It was Marie Curie ___ discoveries changed modern medicine.
explanation: 'Whose discoveries' means 'Marie Curie's discoveries'; 'who's' would mean 'who is'.

sentence: Have you met the couple ___ son is in your class?
hint: the son belongs to the couple
explanation: 'Whose son' means 'their son'; the possessive relative 'whose' is required.

sentence: The photographer ___ camera was damaged is claiming compensation.
explanation: 'Whose' shows that the camera belongs to the photographer; 'who's' means 'who is'.

sentence: We bought a table ___ legs had been damaged in transit.
hint: possession with a thing: the table's legs
explanation: 'Whose' can show possession with things too: 'the table whose legs ...' means 'the table's legs'.

sentence: They lived in a house ___ windows were always shuttered.
hint: the windows belonged to the house
explanation: 'Whose windows' means 'the house's windows'; 'which' cannot show possession directly.

sentence: The committee rejected a plan ___ costs had been underestimated.
explanation: 'Whose costs' means 'the plan's costs'; 'which' would need 'the costs of which'.

sentence: He repaired the car ___ engine had failed.
hint: the engine belongs to the car
explanation: 'Whose engine' means 'the car's engine', showing possession even with objects.

sentence: ___ responsible for locking up tonight?
explanation: 'Who's' is the contraction of 'who is'; 'whose' shows possession and cannot stand before an adjective alone.

sentence: Do you know ___ been invited to the wedding?
explanation: 'Who's' can mean 'who has' in 'who's been invited'; 'whose' would need a noun after it.

sentence: This is the hotel ___ we stayed last summer.
explanation: 'Where' means 'in which' and needs no preposition; 'the hotel which we stayed' would be ungrammatical.

sentence: The cafe ___ we first met has closed down.
hint: location: we met in the cafe
explanation: 'Where' replaces 'in which' for places; 'which' would need a preposition ('in which').

sentence: Is this the street ___ the accident happened?
explanation: 'Where' introduces information about location; 'the street which the accident happened' is wrong.

sentence: The village ___ my grandmother was born has no shops.
explanation: 'Where' is the relative adverb for places; 'which' cannot stand alone here because no preposition is present.

sentence: That's the office ___ I worked for ten years.
explanation: 'Where' means 'in which'; 'I worked the office' shows the place role of the gap.

sentence: The stadium ___ the final will be held holds ninety thousand people.
hint: place adverb inside the relative clause
explanation: 'Where' stands for 'in which place'; 'which' would leave the clause without a subject or object.

sentence: This is the beach ___ we used to play as children.
explanation: 'Where' introduces place information; 'we used to play' already has a subject and object, so 'which' is impossible.

sentence: The restaurant ___ we had dinner last night has excellent reviews.
explanation: 'Where' replaces 'in which' after place nouns; no preposition appears in the clause.

sentence: The country is in a situation ___ an election seems inevitable.
explanation: 'Where' is used with abstract nouns like situation, case and point; 'which' cannot introduce the clause here.

sentence: We have reached the point ___ we must decide whether to continue.
explanation: 'The point where ...' is a standard abstract use of 'where', meaning 'at which'.

sentence: There are cases ___ this rule simply does not apply.
explanation: 'Cases where ...' means 'cases in which ...'; 'that' cannot introduce the clause without a subject.

sentence: The discussion got to a stage ___ nobody was listening any more.
explanation: 'A stage where ...' means 'a stage at which ...'; the clause has its own subject and verb, so 'which' is impossible.

sentence: I'll never forget the day ___ we first met.
explanation: 'When' replaces 'on which' after time nouns like day, year and moment.

sentence: Do you remember the time ___ we got lost in Rome?
explanation: 'When' introduces defining clauses after 'the time'; 'which' would need a preposition.

sentence: The moment ___ she saw the results, she burst into tears.
explanation: 'When' links the moment to the action; 'where' and 'why' do not fit a time noun.

sentence: July and August are the months ___ most Italians take their holidays.
explanation: 'When' means 'in which' after time expressions; the clause describes when the action happens.

sentence: That was the year ___ the company nearly went bankrupt.
hint: time: it happened in that year
explanation: 'When' is used after 'the year'; 'which' would need 'in which'.

sentence: There are times ___ I really miss my home town.
explanation: 'There are times when ...' is a standard pattern; 'when' stands for 'at which'.

sentence: We arrived at the hotel at noon, ___ the rooms were not ready.
explanation: 'When' introduces non-defining clauses about time after a comma; 'that' is impossible after a comma.

sentence: The 1990s was the decade ___ mobile phones became common.
explanation: 'When' replaces 'in which' after time nouns; 'which' cannot stand alone here.

sentence: Nobody knows the reason ___ he resigned so suddenly.
explanation: 'The reason why ...' is the standard pattern; 'why' means 'for which'.

sentence: The reason ___ I'm calling is to confirm your appointment.
explanation: 'The reason why' introduces the explanation or cause; the other options do not express reason.

sentence: Nobody explained the reason ___ the flight was cancelled.
explanation: 'Why' introduces the cause after 'the reason'; it means 'for which'.

sentence: Is there a reason ___ you're behaving so strangely?
explanation: 'A reason why ...' asks about the cause; the other relative words cannot express reason.

sentence: The person to ___ I addressed the letter has moved house.
hint: after a preposition, the object form for people
explanation: After a preposition the object pronoun 'whom' is required for people; 'that' and 'who' cannot follow a preposition.

sentence: Mrs Chan, with ___ I worked for ten years, has retired.
hint: preposition + person in a non-defining clause
explanation: 'With whom' is the formal pattern for people after a preposition; 'with who' and 'with that' are wrong.

sentence: They chose a guide on ___ they could rely completely.
hint: rely on somebody — person after preposition
explanation: After the preposition 'on', the person takes 'whom'; 'which' is only for things.

sentence: The author, about ___ there has been much debate, will speak at the festival.
hint: debate about the author — person after preposition
explanation: 'About whom' is required after the preposition 'about' when referring to a person.

sentence: The manager, for ___ the team played so hard, thanked everyone.
hint: played for the manager — person after preposition
explanation: The preposition 'for' demands the object form 'whom' for a person.

sentence: The lawyers, against ___ the case was brought, denied everything.
hint: the case was brought against them
explanation: 'Against whom' is the formal relative pattern; 'who' and 'that' cannot follow prepositions.

sentence: She has three daughters, all of ___ are at university.
explanation: 'All of whom' refers to people after 'of'; 'all of which' is for things and 'all of them' cannot join the clauses after a comma.

sentence: He is a colleague on ___ you can always depend.
explanation: After 'on', the formal relative pronoun for a person is 'whom'.

sentence: This is the house in ___ I was born.
explanation: 'In which' is the formal pattern; 'in where' does not exist and 'in that' is impossible in relative clauses.

sentence: The chair on ___ the cat was sleeping was my grandmother's.
explanation: 'On which' is the formal pattern for things; 'on where' and 'on that' are not grammatical.

sentence: The exam, the results of ___ will be published on Friday, was very difficult.
hint: quantity noun + of + thing in a non-defining clause
explanation: 'The results of which' joins the clauses formally; 'of whom' is for people and 'of them' cannot link clauses after a comma.

sentence: The tool with ___ I fixed the shelf is in the garage.
explanation: 'With which' is required after the preposition; relative 'that' cannot follow a preposition.

sentence: The bridge, on ___ repairs are still continuing, will reopen in May.
explanation: 'On which' is the formal pattern; 'where' cannot follow a preposition, and 'that' is barred from non-defining clauses.

sentence: The festival, during ___ the town is full of visitors, takes place in July.
hint: preposition + event in a non-defining clause
explanation: 'During which' is the formal pattern; 'during when' does not exist.

sentence: He showed me the drawer in ___ the keys were kept.
explanation: 'In which' is the formal relative pattern for things; 'in where' is ungrammatical.

sentence: The degree to ___ the climate is changing alarms scientists.
explanation: 'The degree to which ...' is a formal pattern used with abstract nouns; 'that' cannot follow the preposition.

sentence: ___ surprised me most was his calm.
hint: 'what' = the thing that; the sentence has no other subject
explanation: 'What' means 'the thing that' and acts as subject: 'What surprised me most ...' — 'that' cannot introduce this nominal clause.

sentence: She told me ___ had happened, but I didn't believe her.
explanation: 'What had happened' means 'the things that had happened'; 'that' cannot stand alone as the subject here.

sentence: Show me ___ you have written so far.
explanation: 'What you have written' means 'the things that you have written'; 'that' cannot head a nominal clause after 'me'.

sentence: We must decide ___ to do next.
explanation: 'What to do' is the standard pattern meaning 'the thing that we should do'.

sentence: That's exactly ___ I needed — thank you!
explanation: 'What I needed' means 'the thing that I needed'; 'that' cannot be used in this free relative position.

sentence: I can't remember ___ happened next.
explanation: 'What happened next' means 'the thing that happened'; 'that' cannot introduce the clause here because the sentence needs a subject inside it.

sentence: This is ___ I meant.
explanation: 'What I meant' means 'the thing that I meant'; 'that I meant' would be an incomplete relative clause.

sentence: Nobody knows ___ caused the fire.
explanation: 'What caused the fire' means 'the thing that caused it'; 'that' cannot act as the subject of this nominal clause.

sentence: Tell me ___ you said to her.
explanation: 'What you said' means 'the words that you said'; 'that' cannot head the clause after 'me'.

sentence: The children were amazed by ___ they saw at the circus.
explanation: 'What they saw' means 'the things that they saw'; after the preposition 'by' only a nominal clause like this fits.

sentence: All ___ glitters is not gold.
hint: after 'all', the relative pronoun is not 'what'
explanation: 'All that glitters' is the proverb pattern; 'what' cannot follow 'all', and 'which' is avoided after 'all'.

sentence: All ___ I want is a quiet weekend at home.
explanation: After 'all' the relative pronoun is 'that' (often omitted); 'all what' is always wrong.

sentence: I've told you everything ___ you need to know.
explanation: After 'everything', 'that' is used (and may be omitted); 'which' is avoided after 'everything'.

sentence: It was the best meal ___ I have ever eaten.
hint: after a superlative, this pronoun is preferred
explanation: After superlatives ('the best ...'), 'that' is the preferred relative pronoun in defining clauses.

sentence: This is the worst storm ___ we have had for years.
hint: after a superlative ('the worst'), use this pronoun
explanation: 'That' follows superlatives in defining relative clauses; 'which' is considered poor style there.

sentence: Have you got anything ___ will remove this stain?
explanation: After 'anything', 'that' is the preferred relative pronoun; 'which' is avoided after -thing words.

sentence: There is nothing ___ I would change about the design.
explanation: After 'nothing', use 'that' (or omit the pronoun); 'which' and 'what' do not fit.

sentence: It is one of the most impressive buildings ___ I have ever seen.
explanation: After superlative expressions, 'that' is the standard relative pronoun in defining clauses.

sentence: There was something ___ smelled awful in the kitchen.
explanation: After 'something', 'that' is the standard relative pronoun; 'what' cannot follow 'something'.

sentence: It was the first time ___ I had ever driven on my own.
hint: after 'the first time', use this pronoun
explanation: 'The first time that ...' is the standard pattern; the pronoun may also be omitted, but 'which' and 'what' do not fit.

sentence: The film, ___ was shot entirely in Iceland, won three awards.
explanation: After a comma, 'that' is impossible: use 'which'.

sentence: The candidate ___ speech impressed us most got the job.
explanation: 'Whose speech' — the speech belonged to the candidate.

sentence: Everything ___ he said turned out to be true.
explanation: After 'everything', the relative is 'that' (or nothing).

sentence: The people ___ live upstairs are very quiet.
explanation: 'Who' is the subject relative for people.

sentence: The assistant ___ I spoke to was extremely helpful.
explanation: 'Whom' is the formal object form after a preposition-style clause.

sentence: 1998 was the year ___ the factory finally closed.
explanation: 'When' introduces the clause of time.

sentence: The reason ___ he resigned was never explained.
explanation: 'The reason why' is the fixed pattern.

sentence: The house ___ windows were broken has now been sold.
explanation: 'Whose windows' — the windows belong to the house.

sentence: My laptop, ___ I bought only last year, has already crashed twice.
explanation: Non-defining clause about a thing: 'which', never 'that'.
